newsitem.title: PERU: Hostage talks in Peru focus on main demand.
newsitem.headline: Hostage talks in Peru focus on main demand.

text.p: Peace brokers in Peru's hostage crisis met with Marxist rebels outside of the Japanese ambassador's residence on Friday as talks to end the 116-day standoff zeroed in on the hostage-takers' main demand.
A white Red Cross car with darkened windows apparently ferried one or more of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) gunmen to talks at a house across the street.
It was thought to be the first time an MRTA representative had left the building for talks since March 12, when formal negotiations with government negotiator Domingo Palermo broke down.

Present at the three-hour meeting was a three-man mediation team of Vatican representative Juan Luis Cipriani, Red Cross official Michel Minnig and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent. Also present was the Japanese government's observer, Terusuke Terada.

Palermo did not attend, but sources said the two sides were engaged in delicate behind-the-scenes negotiations over the rebels' main demand for the freedom of about 450 MRTA fighters in Peruvian jails.
"There is talk of liberation for some of the small fry and reduction of sentences ... some of them may have exaggerated sentences," said a political source close to the government.

Public opinion has backed President Alberto Fujimori's public stance that no MRTA inmates be freed. But the government may be prepared to accept a small political price to avoid bloodshed, the source said.
"If this is the price so that nobody dies, we will pay it," the source said.

About 20 MRTA fighters swept into the Japanese ambassador's home during a cocktail party Dec. 17 and took all 500 guests hostage. They gradually released all but 72 of them, keeping a key list including Peru's foreign minister, Fujimori's brother and top Japanese businessmen.

Despite the appararent deadlock in negotaitions in recent weeks, the political source said both sides remained committed to reaching agreement and that even the MRTA realised its options were limited.
"If they are captured, they will go to jail on life sentences and will never see the sun again. They have to negotiate," he said.
The MRTA is demanding freedom for all 450 of its jailed comrades -- a demand Fujimori has refused, and which sources close to the talks said was a dead issue.

But other concessions may be in the offing, including reduction of sentences for a few convicted rebels and improved prison conditions, sources said. Fujimori has already arranged political assylum for the rebels in Cuba and the Dominican Republic in the event of a peaceful outcome.
Despite the faint signs of progress seen Friday, concern remains high for the health of the 72 men trapped inside the residence for more than 16 weeks without electricity or running water.

"These people (the hostages) cannot remain under this pressure indefinitely," said Congressman Carlos Ferrero Costa, of the ruling Cambio 90 party. "They have practically become prisoners of war and they are not prepared for that," he told Reuters.
Many of the mostly middle-aged men are said to be suffering from stress-related diseases such as high blood pressure, heart and stomach problems.
